entries: From Middle High German -ie, -je, from Latin -ia (feminine singular). Nouns with this Latinate suffix were originally strong (i.e. invariable) feminines, but inflected forms in -ien arose when the distinction between strong and weak feminines collapsed in later Middle High German. These were then treated by analogy with local names like Böhmen, Franken, Sachsen etc. (all originally dative plural of a tribe name).
senses: Used to form the plurals of some neuter nouns of Latin descent whose original plural ends in -ia.

senses: -ing; forms nouns from verbs, usually describing either an event in which an action is carried out, or the result of that action.

entries: From dialectal Middle High German snūben, related to Middle Low German snûven, Middle High German snūfen (“to gasp, pant”), which is part of a group of interrelated forms (see below), ultimately from a Germanic base imitative of the sudden drawing of breath. The verb was originally strong, but developed weak forms as early as the 16th century, which have then predominated since the 18th century. Cognate with Dutch snuiven. Compare also the German variant schnaufen.
senses: to snort; to pant (to breathe loudly)

entries:
Compound of Zange (“(pair of) pliers”) + -n- + Deutsch (“German”), said to have originated or been popularized on Krautchan, a German-language imageboard created in 2007. Due to its lack of archiving, the exact context of its coining is likely undiscoverable. The word is attested by 2011.
A possible motivation for the compound is that it involves intentionally atypical word usage and formation in German, metaphorically using tools to bend words into shape—compare mit der Brechzange, a variation of mit der Brechstange (“forced, by brute force”, literally “with the crowbar”). It could also be a play on Angelsächsisch (“Anglo-Saxon”), reinterpreted as Angel (“fishing rod”) + Sächsisch.
senses: The usage of intentionally overly literal translations and phono-semantic matching of English terminology and slang into German, typically for humorous effect.
